claim: Kinesin-1 is a dimeric motor that transports cargo along microtubules, taking 8.2-nm steps in a hand-over-hand fashion.
source: Kinesin-1 is a dimeric motor that transports cargo along microtubules, taking 8.2-nm steps in a hand-over-hand fashion.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on kinesin structure and function

claim: The ATP hydrolysis cycles of kinesin's two heads are maintained out of phase by a series of gating mechanisms.
source: The ATP hydrolysis cycles of its two heads are maintained out of phase by a series of gating mechanisms, which lead to processive runs averaging ∼1 μm.
evidence: Supported by established understanding of kinesin mechanochemistry and citations

claim: Kinesin's gating mechanisms lead to processive runs averaging approximately 1 μm.
source: The ATP hydrolysis cycles of its two heads are maintained out of phase by a series of gating mechanisms, which lead to processive runs averaging ∼1 μm.
evidence: Supported by established measurements of kinesin processivity

claim: The neck linker (NL) is a key structural element for inter-head coordination in kinesin.
source: A key structural element for inter-head coordination is the neck linker (NL), which connects the heads to the stalk.
evidence: Supported by structural and functional studies of kinesin

claim: The neck linker connects the kinesin heads to the stalk.
source: A key structural element for inter-head coordination is the neck linker (NL), which connects the heads to the stalk.
evidence: Supported by structural knowledge of kinesin architecture

claim: Inter-head tension enhances motor velocity in kinesin.
source: Our results show that, although inter-head tension enhances motor velocity, it is crucial neither for inter-head coordination nor for rapid rear-head release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from NL mutants presented in the manuscript

claim: Inter-head tension is not crucial for inter-head coordination in kinesin.
source: Our results show that, although inter-head tension enhances motor velocity, it is crucial neither for inter-head coordination nor for rapid rear-head release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from NL mutants and modeling

claim: Inter-head tension is not crucial for rapid rear-head release in kinesin.
source: Our results show that, although inter-head tension enhances motor velocity, it is crucial neither for inter-head coordination nor for rapid rear-head release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and kinetic modeling

claim: Cysteine-light mutants do not produce wild-type motility under load.
source: Furthermore, cysteine-light mutants do not produce wild-type motility under load.
evidence: Supported by force-velocity measurements comparing cysteine-light and wild-type constructs

claim: Kinesin-1 is primarily front-head gated.
source: We conclude that kinesin-1 is primarily front-head gated, and that NL length is tuned to enhance unidirectional processivity and velocity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and kinetic modeling showing that rear-head release is not rate-limiting

claim: NL length is tuned to enhance unidirectional processivity and velocity in kinesin.
source: We conclude that kinesin-1 is primarily front-head gated, and that NL length is tuned to enhance unidirectional processivity and velocity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing effects of NL length on processivity and velocity

claim: Kinesin translocates towards the plus-ends of microtubules.
source: Kinesin translocates towards the plus-ends of MTs (Svoboda et al., 1993) via an asymmetric hand-over-hand mechanism (Asbury et al., 2003; Yildiz et al., 2004), hydrolyzing one molecule of ATP (Hua et al., 1997; Schnitzer and Block, 1997; Coy et al., 1999) for each 8.2-nm step (Svoboda et al., 1993) the motor takes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Svoboda et al., 1993

claim: Kinesin uses an asymmetric hand-over-hand mechanism for translocation.
source: Kinesin translocates towards the plus-ends of MTs (Svoboda et al., 1993) via an asymmetric hand-over-hand mechanism (Asbury et al., 2003; Yildiz et al., 2004), hydrolyzing one molecule of ATP (Hua et al., 1997; Schnitzer and Block, 1997; Coy et al., 1999) for each 8.2-nm step (Svoboda et al., 1993) the motor takes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Asbury et al., 2003 and Yildiz et al., 2004

claim: Kinesin hydrolyzes one molecule of ATP for each 8.2-nm step.
source: Kinesin translocates towards the plus-ends of MTs (Svoboda et al., 1993) via an asymmetric hand-over-hand mechanism (Asbury et al., 2003; Yildiz et al., 2004), hydrolyzing one molecule of ATP (Hua et al., 1997; Schnitzer and Block, 1997; Coy et al., 1999) for each 8.2-nm step (Svoboda et al., 1993) the motor takes.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on ATP hydrolysis and stepping

claim: Each kinesin dimer is composed of a pair of identical catalytic motor domains (heads).
source: Each kinesin dimer is composed of a pair of identical catalytic motor domains, or heads, which are connected to a common, coiled-coil stalk by a ∼14-amino-acid-long sequence known as the neck linker (NL) (Kozielski et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kozielski et al., 1997 and structural knowledge

claim: The kinesin heads are connected to a common, coiled-coil stalk by a ~14-amino-acid-long neck linker.
source: Each kinesin dimer is composed of a pair of identical catalytic motor domains, or heads, which are connected to a common, coiled-coil stalk by a ∼14-amino-acid-long sequence known as the neck linker (NL) (Kozielski et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kozielski et al., 1997

claim: During the mechanochemical cycle, each kinesin head transitions between states that are strongly bound to the MT (ATP-containing state and no-nucleotide state) and states that are weakly bound to the MT (ADP-containing state).
source: During the mechanochemical cycle, each kinesin head transitions between one or more states that are strongly bound to the MT (the ATP-containing state, and also the no-nucleotide state), and one or more states that are weakly bound to the MT (the ADP-containing state) (Block, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Block, 2007 and established mechanochemical understanding

claim: The kinesin mechanochemical cycle begins with the one-head-bound (1-HB), ATP-waiting state where the nucleotide-free front head is strongly bound to the MT while the rear, ADP-bound tethered head remains unbound.
source: A simplified version of this cycle (Figure 1A) may arbitrarily be taken to begin with the one-head-bound (1-HB), ATP-waiting state [α], where the nucleotide-free front head is strongly bound to the MT while the rear, ADP-bound tethered head remains unbound (Hackney, 1994; Asenjo and Sosa, 2009; Guydosh and Block, 2009; Toprak et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the mechanochemical cycle

claim: Following ATP binding to the MT-bound head, the neck linker undergoes a structural reconfiguration and forms a β-sheet with the head in a process termed NL docking.
source: Following ATP binding to the MT-bound head, the NL of its motor domain undergoes a structural reconfiguration and forms a β-sheet with the head, in a process termed NL docking (Rice et al., 1999; Schnitzer et al., 2000; Rosenfeld et al., 2001; Asenjo et al., 2006; Tomishige et al., 2006; Khalil et al., 2008; Sindelar and Downing, 2010; Clancy et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations on NL docking

claim: NL docking shifts the position of the tethered head towards the MT plus-end, beyond the position of the bound head.
source: NL docking shifts the position of the tethered head towards the MT plus-end, beyond the position of the bound head [β1, β2].
evidence: Supported by structural and mechanistic understanding of kinesin stepping

claim: NL docking may occur in two stages: first, ATP binding induces a load-dependent mechanical transition leading to partial NL docking, whereas subsequent ATP hydrolysis completes the docking and enables the tethered head to bind the MT.
source: Recent work has suggested that NL docking may occur in two stages: first, ATP binding induces a load-dependent mechanical transition, leading to partial NL docking [β1], whereas subsequent ATP hydrolysis completes the docking and enables the tethered head to bind the MT [β2] (Milic et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milic et al., 2014

claim: Once the bound head hydrolyzes ATP, fully docks its NL, and the tethered head binds the MT, the motor enters a mechanically strained, two-heads-bound (2-HB) state.
source: Once the bound head hydrolyzes ATP, fully docks its NL, and the tethered head binds the MT, the motor enters a mechanically strained, two-heads-bound (2-HB) state [γ] (Rice et al., 1999; Rosenfeld et al., 2003; Block, 2007; Yildiz et al., 2008; Gennerich and Vale, 2009; Clancy et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations on the 2-HB state

claim: Rear-head release completes the step and returns the motor to its initial 1-HB waiting state, having translocated forward by one step (8.2 nm) along the MT.
source: Finally, rear-head release (Klumpp et al., 2004) completes the step and returns the motor to its initial 1-HB waiting state [α], primed to begin the cycle anew, after having translocated forward by one step (8.2 nm) along the MT.
evidence: Supported by citation and mechanistic understanding

claim: The processivity of kinesin relies upon a tight coordination of biochemical and mechanical events, collectively known as gating mechanisms.
source: The processivity of kinesin—evinced by the ability of a single dimer to undergo >100 consecutive stepping cycles before dissociation—relies upon a tight coordination of the biochemical and mechanical events, collectively known as gating mechanisms (Block, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Block, 2007 and established understanding of kinesin processivity

claim: A single kinesin dimer can undergo more than 100 consecutive stepping cycles before dissociation.
source: The processivity of kinesin—evinced by the ability of a single dimer to undergo >100 consecutive stepping cycles before dissociation—relies upon a tight coordination of the biochemical and mechanical events, collectively known as gating mechanisms (Block, 2007).
evidence: Supported by established measurements of kinesin processivity

claim: DmK-WT and constructs with NLs extended by up to 3 AA displayed a 50% reduction in fluorescence following the addition of MTs in mantADP release experiments.
source: Wild-type (WT) Drosophila kinesin (DmK-WT), as well as constructs with NLs extended by up to 3 AA, displayed a 50% reduction in fluorescence following the addition of MTs (Figure 2A), consistent with being in a 1-HB state, where only one of the two heads is bound to the MT and releases mantADP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: A 50% reduction in fluorescence in mantADP release experiments is consistent with kinesin being in a 1-HB state.
source: Wild-type (WT) Drosophila kinesin (DmK-WT), as well as constructs with NLs extended by up to 3 AA, displayed a 50% reduction in fluorescence following the addition of MTs (Figure 2A), consistent with being in a 1-HB state, where only one of the two heads is bound to the MT and releases mantADP.
evidence: Supported by interpretation of fluorescence data based on established assay principles

claim: Constructs with NL inserts of 4, 5, or 6 AA exhibited progressively greater drops in fluorescence upon the addition of MTs, corresponding to 16% of DmK-4AA, 38% of DmK-5AA, and 65% of DmK-6AA motors releasing mantADP from both heads.
source: By contrast, constructs with NL inserts consisting of 4, 5, or 6 AA exhibited progressively greater drops in fluorescence upon the addition of MTs (Figure 2A). These decreases correspond to 16% of DmK-4AA, 38% of DmK-5AA, and 65% of DmK-6AA motors releasing mantADP from both heads, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: MantADP exchange experiments revealed an order-of-magnitude increase in exchange rate relative to WT kinesin once the NL domain was extended by 4 or more AA.
source: Additional mantADP exchange experiments—where the frequency of transient rear-head interactions with the MT was assessed based on the effective rate of mantADP exchange at the rear head—revealed an order-of-magnitude increase relative to WT kinesin once the NL domain was extended by 4 or more AA (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Kinesin can maintain a stable, 1-HB ATP-waiting state with up to 3 additional AA in its NL.
source: Taken all together, these results indicate that kinesin can maintain a stable, 1-HB ATP-waiting state with up to 3 additional AA in its NL, but that extending the NL by 4 AA or more leads to an abrupt increase in rebinding of the rear-head to the MT.
evidence: Supported by mantADP release and exchange data

claim: Extending the NL by 4 AA or more leads to an abrupt increase in rebinding of the rear-head to the MT.
source: Taken all together, these results indicate that kinesin can maintain a stable, 1-HB ATP-waiting state with up to 3 additional AA in its NL, but that extending the NL by 4 AA or more leads to an abrupt increase in rebinding of the rear-head to the MT.
evidence: Supported by mantADP release and exchange data

claim: Extending the NL by just a single AA decreased the unloaded run length by a factor of ~3 relative to the WT run length.
source: Extending the NL by just a single AA decreased the unloaded run length by a factor of ∼3 relative to the WT run length.
evidence: Supported by run length measurements shown in Figure 3

claim: Further increments in the NL length (up to 6 AA) yielded only minor decreases in run length relative to DmK-1AA.
source: Further increments in the NL length (up to 6 AA) yielded only minor decreases in run length relative to DmK-1AA (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by run length data shown in Figure 3

claim: Under unloaded conditions, DmK-6AA was capable of taking several dozen consecutive forward steps, on average, before dissociating.
source: Under unloaded conditions, DmK-6AA was capable of taking several dozen consecutive forward steps, on average, before dissociating, indicating that kinesin retains significant processivity with as many as 6 AA introduced into its NL.
evidence: Supported by run length measurements

claim: Kinesin retains significant processivity with as many as 6 AA introduced into its NL.
source: Under unloaded conditions, DmK-6AA was capable of taking several dozen consecutive forward steps, on average, before dissociating, indicating that kinesin retains significant processivity with as many as 6 AA introduced into its NL.
evidence: Supported by run length measurements

claim: The differences in processivity among constructs with differing NL lengths were substantially more pronounced under hindering forces than under assisting forces.
source: In the presence of forces applied either against (hindering loads) or along (assisting loads) the direction of kinesin motility (Figure 3, inset), the differences in processivity among constructs with differing NL lengths were substantially more pronounced under hindering forces than under assisting forces.
evidence: Supported by run length data under different loads shown in Figure 3

claim: A gradual, exponential decrease in run length was observed for all constructs under increasing hindering loads.
source: A gradual, exponential decrease in run length was observed for all constructs under increasing hindering loads, but the application of even a small assisting force (+2 pN) abruptly reduced the run length for both the WT and NL-mutant constructs.
evidence: Supported by run length data shown in Figure 3

claim: The application of even a small assisting force (+2 pN) abruptly reduced the run length for both the WT and NL-mutant constructs.
source: A gradual, exponential decrease in run length was observed for all constructs under increasing hindering loads, but the application of even a small assisting force (+2 pN) abruptly reduced the run length for both the WT and NL-mutant constructs.
evidence: Supported by run length data shown in Figure 3

claim: The characteristic distance parameter for the force dependence of run length (δL) was nearly an order of magnitude greater under hindering-load conditions than under assisting-load conditions for all constructs.
source: Based on exponential fits to the mean run lengths as a function of applied load, the characteristic distance parameter for the force dependence of run length, δL, was nearly an order of magnitude greater under hindering-load conditions than under assisting-load conditions for all constructs (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by exponential fits to run length data shown in Table 1

claim: The highly asymmetric force dependence of DmK run lengths previously reported for the WT motor is also exhibited by kinesin constructs with NLs extended up to 6 AA.
source: These results show that the highly asymmetric force dependence of DmK run lengths previously reported for the WT motor (Milic et al., 2014) is also exhibited by kinesin constructs with NLs extended up to 6 AA.
evidence: Supported by run length data and comparison to previous work

claim: The distance parameters for both hindering and assisting loads were nearly independent of NL length.
source: Interestingly, although processivity was found to depend upon the NL length, particularly under hindering-load and unloaded conditions, the distance parameters for both hindering and assisting loads were nearly independent of NL length (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by parameter values shown in Table 1

claim: Under saturating levels of ATP, the addition of Pi increased the DmK-6AA run length relative to that in its absence.
source: Under saturating levels of ATP, the addition of Pi increased the DmK-6AA run length relative to that in its absence (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: No statistically significant changes in processivity were detected at low ATP concentrations, nor under conditions where ATP was replaced with ATPγS, nor in the presence of 100 mM potassium chloride for DmK-6AA.
source: However, no statistically significant changes in processivity were detected at low ATP concentrations, nor under conditions where ATP was replaced with the slowly hydrolyzable analog, ATPγS, nor in the presence of 100 mM potassium chloride (used as a control for ionic strength effects) (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Run lengths under otherwise identical assay conditions were systematically lower for DmK-6AA than for DmK-WT.
source: Although run lengths under otherwise identical assay conditions were systematically lower for DmK-6AA than for DmK-WT, those differences disappeared when the data were normalized relative to the baseline run lengths (no added Pi) for each motor (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: When run length data were normalized relative to baseline run lengths, the differences between DmK-6AA and DmK-WT disappeared.
source: Although run lengths under otherwise identical assay conditions were systematically lower for DmK-6AA than for DmK-WT, those differences disappeared when the data were normalized relative to the baseline run lengths (no added Pi) for each motor (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by normalized data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Both WT and mutant constructs exhibited a force-velocity relationship that is highly asymmetric with respect to the direction of the applied load.
source: Both WT and mutant constructs exhibited a force–velocity relationship that is highly asymmetric with respect to the direction of the applied load (Figure 5), consistent with previous findings (Block et al., 2003; Block, 2007).
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figure 5 and citations to previous work

claim: The insertion of a single AA in the NL elicited a drop in velocity across all loads.
source: Whereas the insertion of a single AA in the NL elicited a drop in velocity across all loads, additional NL insertions produced no further changes in velocity: indeed, Drosophila kinesin stepped at significant rates with as many as 6 additional AA in its NL.
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figure 5

claim: Additional NL insertions beyond 1 AA produced no further changes in velocity.
source: Whereas the insertion of a single AA in the NL elicited a drop in velocity across all loads, additional NL insertions produced no further changes in velocity: indeed, Drosophila kinesin stepped at significant rates with as many as 6 additional AA in its NL.
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figure 5

claim: Drosophila kinesin stepped at significant rates with as many as 6 additional AA in its NL.
source: Whereas the insertion of a single AA in the NL elicited a drop in velocity across all loads, additional NL insertions produced no further changes in velocity: indeed, Drosophila kinesin stepped at significant rates with as many as 6 additional AA in its NL.
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figure 5

claim: DmK-WT is not sped up by assisting loads.
source: In contrast to DmK-WT, which is not sped up by assisting loads, the reduction in unloaded velocity produced by NL extension could be recovered by applying larger assisting loads (∼20 pN).
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figure 5

claim: The reduction in unloaded velocity produced by NL extension could be recovered by applying larger assisting loads (~20 pN).
source: In contrast to DmK-WT, which is not sped up by assisting loads, the reduction in unloaded velocity produced by NL extension could be recovered by applying larger assisting loads (∼20 pN).
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figure 5

claim: The inter-head tension in WT kinesin (Fi,WT) is 26 ± 3 pN in the 2-HB state.
source: With this assumption, we determined the inter-head tension in WT kinesin (Fi,WT) to be 26 ± 3 pN in the 2-HB state, a value that agrees well with molecular dynamics simulations, which predicted that it would lie in the range of 15–35 pN (Hariharan and Hancock, 2009).
evidence: Supported by modeling of velocity data and comparison to molecular dynamics simulations

claim: The unloaded rate of rear-head release is 260 ± 10 s⁻¹.
source: The model fit also supplies an estimate of the unloaded rate of rear-head release, 260 ± 10 s−1.
evidence: Supported by modeling of velocity data

claim: Inter-head tension alone is capable of increasing the rate of rear-head release by an order of magnitude.
source: With the derived values for Fi,WT and the load-dependence of rear-head unbinding, δ3, the expression for k3 shows that inter-head tension alone is capable of increasing the rate of rear-head release by an order of magnitude (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Table 2

claim: The modeled rate of ATP hydrolysis (plus other primarily biochemical events) is 95 ± 1 s⁻¹.
source: Moreover, the modeled rate of ATP hydrolysis (plus the other primarily biochemical events, above), 95 ± 1 s−1, is consistent with previous estimates of the hydrolysis rate from both biochemical and single-molecule studies (Ma and Taylor, 1997; Gilbert et al., 1998; Schnitzer et al., 2000; Farrell et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by modeling and comparison to previous studies

claim: Under all practical loads, hydrolysis is substantially slower than rear-head release.
source: Under all practical loads, hydrolysis is substantially slower than rear-head release.
evidence: Supported by comparison of modeled rates k2 and k3

claim: The 26-pN inter-head tension in WT kinesin can enhance the rate of front-head release at the unbinding gate by a factor of ~50.
source: From these numbers, it follows that the 26-pN inter-head tension in WT kinesin can enhance the rate of front-head release at the unbinding gate by a factor of ∼50.
evidence: Supported by unbinding rate measurements and calculations

claim: The unloaded release rate for front-head detachment under hindering loads is 1.11 ± 0.03 s⁻¹.
source: The unbinding rate for all hindering loads (koff−) is determined by koff−0=1.11±0.03 s−1 and δoff−=0.60±0.01 nm (fitting the unbinding rates only to data from superstall forces yielded nearly identical parameter values).
evidence: Supported by exponential fits to unbinding data shown in Figure 6

claim: The distance parameter for front-head detachment under hindering loads is 0.60 ± 0.01 nm.
source: The unbinding rate for all hindering loads (koff−) is determined by koff−0=1.11±0.03 s−1 and δoff−=0.60±0.01 nm (fitting the unbinding rates only to data from superstall forces yielded nearly identical parameter values).
evidence: Supported by exponential fits to unbinding data shown in Figure 6

claim: DmK-6AA exhibits a substantially greater velocity than HsK-CL-6AA.
source: The force–velocity relation for DmK-6AA (Figure 5), which carries the insert LQASQT in its NL, differs significantly from the corresponding relation for a human (HsK) cysteine-light (CL) construct (Rice et al., 1999) with the insert AEQKLT, HsK-CL-6AA (Clancy et al., 2011) (Figure 7). Specifically, DmK-6AA exhibits a substantially greater velocity—which is also less force dependent—than HsK-CL-6AA (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of velocity data shown in Figures 5 and 7

claim: DmK-6AA velocity is less force dependent than HsK-CL-6AA.
source: Specifically, DmK-6AA exhibits a substantially greater velocity—which is also less force dependent—than HsK-CL-6AA (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of velocity data shown in Figure 7A

claim: HsK-CL-6AA was capable of undertaking many rearward steps when subjected to hindering loads beyond the stall force.
source: Whereas HsK-CL-6AA was capable of undertaking many rearward steps when subjected to hindering loads beyond the stall force (Clancy et al., 2011), no such processive backstepping was observed for DmK-6AA, nor for any other Drosophila constructs examined that retained native cysteine residues.
evidence: Supported by citation to Clancy et al., 2011

claim: No processive backstepping was observed for DmK-6AA or any other Drosophila constructs examined that retained native cysteine residues.
source: Whereas HsK-CL-6AA was capable of undertaking many rearward steps when subjected to hindering loads beyond the stall force (Clancy et al., 2011), no such processive backstepping was observed for DmK-6AA, nor for any other Drosophila constructs examined that retained native cysteine residues.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The wild-type forms of Drosophila (DmK-WT) and human (HsK-WT) kinesin exhibit nearly identical force-velocity relations under otherwise identical conditions.
source: By contrast, the wild-type forms of Drosophila (DmK-WT) and human (HsK-WT) kinesin exhibit nearly identical force–velocity relations under otherwise identical conditions (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Under hindering loads, both HsK-CL and DmK-CL were appreciably slower and more sensitive to load than either DmK-WT or the corresponding truncated human construct, HsK-WT.
source: Under hindering loads, both HsK-CL and DmK-CL were appreciably slower, and also more sensitive to load, than either DmK-WT or the corresponding truncated human construct, HsK-WT.
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The human CL construct can be sped up under assisting loads by as much as 200 nm/s.
source: For the case of the human CL construct, the entire shape of the force–velocity relation is affected, because this motor can be sped up under assisting loads by as much as 200 nm/s.
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figure 7B

claim: WT motors do not exhibit speed-up under assisting loads.
source: WT motors do not exhibit this effect, and it suggests that important steps in the mechanochemical cycle have been altered in the mutant.
evidence: Supported by velocity data comparisons

claim: A single CL mutation (C338S) in the NL can account for some, but not all, of the change in force dependence under hindering loads.
source: Comparison shows that this single mutation can account for some, but not all, of the change in force dependence under hindering loads (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by velocity data for DmK-C338S shown in Figure 7B

claim: A single CL mutation in the NL cannot alone account for the differences between WT and CL motors.
source: This indicates that a single CL mutation in the NL cannot alone account for the differences between WT and CL motors.
evidence: Supported by comparison of DmK-C338S and DmK-CL velocity data

claim: With the same insert sequences, human constructs were systematically slower than the corresponding Drosophila constructs.
source: Although the force–velocity curves for DmK-WT and HsK-WT are practically indistinguishable, extending the NL of these motors by 6 AA, using either the sequence LQASQT or AEQKLT, showed that with the same insert sequences, human constructs were systematically slower than the corresponding Drosophila constructs (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figures 7C and 7D

claim: NL extensions based on AEQKLT produced motors that were slower than the corresponding constructs based on LQASQT, for both DmK and HsK.
source: Furthermore, NL extensions based on AEQKLT produced motors that were slower than the corresponding constructs based on LQASQT, for both DmK and HsK (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: Supported by velocity data shown in Figures 7E and 7F

claim: None of the mutants with extended NL domains that retained their native cysteine residues exhibited processive backstepping under superstall loads.
source: Nevertheless, regardless of species or insert sequence, none of the mutants with extended NL domains that retained their native cysteine residues exhibited either processive backstepping under superstall loads or velocities surpassing the WT under assisting loads.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations across all constructs

claim: None of the mutants with extended NL domains that retained their native cysteine residues exhibited velocities surpassing the WT under assisting loads.
source: Nevertheless, regardless of species or insert sequence, none of the mutants with extended NL domains that retained their native cysteine residues exhibited either processive backstepping under superstall loads or velocities surpassing the WT under assisting loads.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations across all constructs

claim: The stepping gate is not strongly influenced by NL length.
source: Because WT and mutant constructs with as many as three additional AA in the NL can maintain a stable 1-HB ATP-waiting state, our results show that the stepping gate is not strongly influenced by NL length.
evidence: Supported by mantADP release data

claim: The stepping gate is clearly compromised in constructs with longer NL inserts (4-6 AA).
source: Although the stepping gate is clearly compromised in constructs with longer NL inserts (4–6 AA), a substantial portion of the population retains mantADP in its rear head (Figure 2A), suggesting that gating is not abolished even in these motors.
evidence: Supported by mantADP release data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Gating is not abolished even in motors with 4-6 AA NL inserts.
source: Although the stepping gate is clearly compromised in constructs with longer NL inserts (4–6 AA), a substantial portion of the population retains mantADP in its rear head (Figure 2A), suggesting that gating is not abolished even in these motors.
evidence: Supported by mantADP release and exchange data

claim: The length of the wild-type NL domain may be near optimal for maximizing motor processivity.
source: We conclude that the length of the wild-type NL domain may be near optimal for maximizing motor processivity.
evidence: Supported by run length data showing dramatic decrease with 1 AA extension and previous work showing non-processivity with 1 AA shortening

claim: The decrease in run length associated with extended NLs arises from the corresponding increase in the diffusive space that the tethered head must explore before reaching its next MT binding site.
source: We speculate that the decrease in run length associated with extended NLs (Figure 3) arises from the corresponding increase in the diffusive space that the tethered head must explore before reaching its next MT binding site.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed run length decrease

claim: Enlarging the diffusive space extends the time that the tethered head takes to reach the forward site, thereby increasing the probability that the partner head may release the MT prematurely, enhancing dimer dissociation.
source: Enlarging that space extends the time that the tethered head takes to reach the forward site, thereby increasing the probability that the partner head may release the MT prematurely, enhancing dimer dissociation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation

claim: The rates of any biochemical events associated with the bound head, when the kinesin cycle is at the binding gate, are independent of the NL length.
source: The finding that normalized run lengths for the NL constructs were identical under all conditions tested (Figure 4B) suggests that the rates of any biochemical events associated with the bound head, when the kinesin cycle is at the binding gate, are independent of the NL length.
evidence: Inferred from normalized run length data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Inserting a single AA into the NL introduces sufficient slack into the inter-head linkage that any further extensions become superfluous.
source: We surmise that inserting a single AA into the NL introduces sufficient slack into the inter-head linkage that any further extensions become superfluous.
evidence: Inferred from velocity data showing no further changes beyond 1 AA insertion

claim: A relatively high inter-head tension (26 ± 3 pN) may be advantageous in tuning WT kinesin for increased velocity.
source: A relatively high inter-head tension (26 ± 3 pN; Table 2) may be advantageous in tuning WT kinesin for increased velocity.
evidence: Inferred from modeling results and velocity comparisons

claim: Inter-head tension plays only a modulatory role in kinesin motility.
source: However, because constructs with up to 6 AA inserted in the NL retained significant functionality (Figure 5), we infer that inter-head tension plays only a modulatory role in kinesin motility, a conclusion that gains support from the modeled force–velocity relations (Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from functionality of extended NL constructs and modeling

claim: The 2-HB state of kinesin is primarily front-head gated, in the sense that the kinetic cycle of the front head is slowed while the rear head remains MT-bound.
source: We find instead that the 2-HB state of kinesin is primarily front-head gated, in the sense that the kinetic cycle of the front head is slowed while the rear head remains MT-bound.
evidence: Inferred from modeling showing rear-head release is not rate-limiting

claim: The gating mechanism responsible for processivity in the 2-HB state does not require inter-head tension, but rather occurs through a modulation of the rates of biochemical processes occurring at the front head.
source: Put another way, the gating mechanism responsible for processivity in the 2-HB state does not require inter-head tension, but rather occurs through a modulation of the rates of biochemical processes occurring at the front head, including ATP hydrolysis, and possibly productive ATP binding (Clancy et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from modeling and experimental data

claim: Kinesin is negatively rear-head gated at the 2-HB state: the presence of inter-head tension serves to undermine any contribution of the unbinding gate in maintaining processive motility.
source: Kinesin is, in this sense, negatively rear-head gated at the 2-HB state: if anything, the presence of inter-head tension serves to undermine any contribution of the unbinding gate in maintaining processive motility.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of how inter-head tension affects front vs rear head detachment

claim: It is unlikely that inter-head tension functions as the primary mechanism for head coordination in the kinesin cycle.
source: Because inter-head tension adversely affects processivity from the 2-HB state, and because the rate of rear-head release is not rate limiting for the kinesin cycle even in the absence of inter-head tension, we conclude that it is unlikely to function as the primary mechanism for head coordination in the kinesin cycle.
evidence: Inferred from modeling and experimental data

claim: It is the spatial orientation of the NL (pointing forward in the docked state and rearward when undocked), rather than inter-head tension per se, that facilitates coordination of biochemical states.
source: However, as we have previously argued (Clancy et al., 2011), results from the earlier studies can be reconciled with our own by invoking a front-head gating mechanism for kinesin where it is the spatial orientation of the NL (i.e., pointing forward in the docked state and rearward when undocked), rather than inter-head tension, per se, that facilitates coordination of biochemical states, as discussed (Asenjo et al., 2003; Hahlen et al., 2006; Clancy et al., 2011).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on previous work and current data

claim: Gating at the 2-HB state may be accomplished not by accelerating rates associated with the rear head, but by inhibiting—via the spatial orientation of the NL—the ATP hydrolysis cycle at the front head, until the rear head detaches.
source: In other words, gating at the 2-HB state may be accomplished not by accelerating rates associated with the rear head, but by inhibiting—via the spatial orientation of the NL—the ATP hydrolysis cycle at the front head, until the rear head detaches.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental and modeling data

claim: The processive backstepping behavior of HsK-CL-6AA arises from some combination of NL extension and the introduction of one or more of the seven mutations used to produce human CL kinesin.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that the processive backstepping behavior of HsK-CL-6AA arises from some combination of NL extension and the introduction of one or more of the seven mutations used to produce human CL kinesin.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of different constructs

claim: The key role played by NL length in kinesin gating is twofold: (1) to enhance processivity by facilitating binding of the tethered head to the forward MT site at the binding gate, and (2) to increase velocity by accelerating rear-head release from the 2-HB state at the unbinding gate.
source: We conclude that the key role played by NL length in kinesin gating is twofold: (1) to enhance processivity by facilitating binding of the tethered head to the forward MT site at the binding gate, and (2) to increase velocity by accelerating rear-head release from the 2-HB state at the unbinding gate.
evidence: Conclusion based on all experimental and modeling data

claim: The kinesin-1 nanomechanical properties appear to be selected for processivity and velocity.
source: In general, the kinesin-1 nanomechanical properties appear to be selected for processivity and velocity.
evidence: General conclusion based on all findings

claim: The dominant effect of lengthening the NL is to compromise the binding gate.
source: An explanation is that the dominant effect of lengthening the NL is to compromise the binding gate, and that the deleterious effect of NL length at this gate outweighs any compensating effects of reduced inter-head tension at the unbinding gate.
evidence: Inferred from run length and velocity data
